title: Promote talos01 + talos03 to control-plane (3-master HA)
description:
Current cluster is single-CP: talos00 only. Any disk corruption, kernel
panic, or hardware failure on talos00 = full cluster outage with no fast
recovery path (UPS-2026-05-09 was this exact scenario).

Per ADR-001 (docs/02-architecture/ADR-001-power-resilience.md), the
recommended HA layout is **talos00 + talos01 + talos03** as control planes,
with talos02-gpu and talos06 remaining pure workers. Rationale:

- talos02 (Intel Ultra 5 + Intel Arc GPU) is too capable to "waste" on CP
- talos06 (Intel Arc GPU node) same reasoning
- talos01 (Ryzen 5800U) and talos03 (Ryzen 5800U, mostly idle per
  docs/05-projects/cluster-optimization/) are strong CP candidates

## Procedure

1. **Generate** new control-plane machine configs for talos01 + talos03:
   ```
   task talos:gen-config   # if existing, OR
   talosctl gen config catalyst-cluster https://192.168.1.54:6443 ...
   ```
   Adjust each to keep the node's IP + factory installer URL +
   schematic with iscsi-tools (and amd-ucode/amdgpu for talos03).

2. **Apply** via `talosctl apply-config` (triggers reinstall + reboot).
   Do ONE at a time, verifying etcd quorum forms before doing the next:
   - First: talos01 → wait for etcd member added, quorum at 2/2
   - Then:  talos03 → wait for etcd member added, quorum at 3/3

3. **Verify**:
   - `kubectl get nodes` shows 3 control-plane roles
   - `talosctl --nodes <each-cp> etcd status` shows all 3 as healthy
   - `talosctl health` returns OK
   - All workloads still running (CP nodes should still accept workloads
     since allowSchedulingOnControlPlanes=true per CLAUDE.md)

4. **Document**: update docs/02-architecture/ with new topology;
   update CLAUDE.md "Multi-Node Cluster" section.

## Test value

After promotion:
- `talosctl --nodes 192.168.1.54 upgrade --preserve=true` should work
  WITHOUT taking down the whole cluster (other CPs absorb the load)
- Rolling Talos upgrades become trivial via upgrade-talos.py
- Disk failure on one CP = cluster keeps running (etcd 2/3 quorum)

## Risks

- Each `apply-config` is a node rebuild — workloads on that node briefly
  disrupted (drain + reboot). Talos handles this for us.
- If etcd quorum doesn't form correctly, we're in worse shape than before.
  Mitigation: take etcd snapshot BEFORE starting (`talosctl etcd snapshot`).
- talos01/talos03 must have their existing extensions preserved (per
  TALOS-6od learnings). Use their existing factory installer URLs.

## Out of scope

- UPS graceful-shutdown integration — separate ticket
- ext4 ephemeral migration (deferred per ADR-001)

Split out from: TALOS-asv
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] etcd snapshot taken before any change (talosctl etcd snapshot)
- [ ] talos01 promoted to control-plane (kubectl shows role)
- [ ] talos03 promoted to control-plane (kubectl shows role)
- [ ] talosctl etcd status shows 3 healthy members from each CP
- [ ] talosctl health returns OK from each CP endpoint
- [ ] All existing workloads still running (no PVC issues)
- [ ] talos01 + talos03 retain their factory installer schematics
      (iscsi-tools, amd-ucode/amdgpu for talos03)
- [ ] Validate a rolling CP upgrade works: upgrade talos01 to a new
      patch version while talos00 + talos03 serve the cluster
- [ ] Documentation updated: docs/02-architecture/ topology + CLAUDE.md
notes: Parent: TALOS-asv (ADR-001 written). Defense-in-depth for non-power failures.

title: UPS graceful-shutdown integration (NUT or SNMP → talosctl shutdown)
description:
Hardware UPS swap is done (TALOS-asv), but the cluster still has no automated
graceful-shutdown path when UPS battery runs low. Without this, the next
power event will replay UPS-2026-05-09: unclean shutdown → XFS corruption →
total state loss on local-path PVCs (TSDB, Grafana, Nexus, MongoDB, etc.).

Per ADR-001 (docs/02-architecture/ADR-001-power-resilience.md), this is the
HIGHEST-LEVERAGE defense — addresses the root cause of the 2026-05-09 outage
directly, even before HA control plane work.

## Approach options

Pick one based on the new UPS's capabilities:

### Option A: SNMP / HTTP webhook (cleanest)
- If the new UPS has a network management card (NMC) — it exposes battery
  state via SNMP or HTTP.
- A small in-cluster pod polls UPS battery level on a CronJob or watcher
  pattern, and on low-battery calls the Talos API to shutdown.
- Auth via talosctl certs mounted as Secret.

### Option B: NUT (Network UPS Tools) on a Pi/external host
- Standard pattern. Pi (or any always-on Linux box) connects to UPS via
  USB, runs NUT server, monitors battery.
- On low-battery, NUT script SSHes to admin host or hits a webhook that
  triggers `talosctl shutdown`.
- More moving parts but works with any USB UPS.

### Option C: NUT client DaemonSet on Talos
- Talos doesn't expose /dev/usb out-of-the-box; would need a system
  extension or a host-network sidecar with special privileges.
- Complicated; only pursue if A and B aren't feasible.

## What to do FIRST

1. Identify the new UPS make/model
2. Check if it has SNMP, HTTP API, or just USB
3. Pick A or B accordingly
4. Build the monitoring component
5. Test by deliberately draining battery to trigger low-battery threshold
   (or simulate via mock signal)

## Out of scope

- Replacing UPS hardware (already done)
- 3-master HA — separate ticket
- ext4 ephemeral filesystem migration (deferred per ADR-001)

Split out from: TALOS-asv
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Identify new UPS model + supported monitoring protocols documented
- [ ] Approach chosen (A/B/C) with rationale recorded in this ticket
- [ ] Monitoring component built and deployed
- [ ] Talos API auth for shutdown verified (talosctl + cert)
- [ ] Test: simulated low-battery triggers graceful shutdown of all 5 nodes
      in the correct order (workers parallel → control plane last,
      same as scripts/shutdown-cluster.sh)
- [ ] Runbook entry added to docs/05-runbooks/ describing manual override +
      testing procedure

title: Cilium BPF policy map overflow + cascading meltdown (2026-05-21)
description:
Following the Talos v1.13.2 upgrade on 2026-05-21, a sequence of cascading failures took the control plane offline for ~40 minutes. Root cause: long-broken opentelemetry-operator (12+ days in CrashLoopBackOff due to orphan ServiceMonitor) whose MutatingWebhookConfiguration was still registered with failurePolicy=Fail. When we restarted the Cilium DaemonSet to apply a separate BPF map-size fix, every new pod admission stalled on the dead webhook, preventing Cilium agents from starting, which broke apiserver networking, which broke everything.

The actual change (BPF map size bump 16384 → 65536) was correct and necessary. The trigger was *how* it was applied (DS rollout restart) interacting with the latent webhook bug.

Full post-mortem: docs/06-troubleshooting/2026-05-21-cilium-cascading-meltdown.md

Commits landed (844aa94):
- configs/cilium-values.yaml + cilium-manifest.yaml: BPF policy map → 65536
- scripts/upgrade-talos.py: pre-flight webhook health check
- scripts/shutdown-cluster.sh: pre-flight webhook health check
- infrastructure/.../otel-operator/helmrelease.yaml: failurePolicy=Ignore + namespaceSelector
- docs/05-runbooks/cluster-bootstrap.md: sizing considerations
- docs/06-troubleshooting/2026-05-21-cilium-cascading-meltdown.md: full retro

- [x] Webhook health check added to upgrade-talos.py

title: Traefik TLSStore default rejected: knowledgedump-wildcard-tls secret missing
description:
Traefik logs continually emit:

  ERR Secret traefik/knowledgedump-wildcard-tls does not exist TLSStore=default namespace=traefik providerName=kubernetescrd

Cause: the Certificate `knowledgedump-wildcard` in the `traefik` namespace has been Ready=False for >17h. cert-manager has the in-progress secret `knowledgedump-wildcard-r7knw` (Opaque, not yet promoted to `kubernetes.io/tls` named `knowledgedump-wildcard-tls`) because the Cloudflare DNS-01 challenge keeps failing with:

  while querying the Cloudflare API for DELETE "/zones//dns_records/71352d7ed4a669c68feff6281ab78a2a"
  Error: 7003: Could not route to /client/v4/zones/dns_records/...

(Empty zone in URL — cert-manager couldn't resolve the Cloudflare zone ID.)

Because the `defaultCertificate` of the `default` TLSStore points at the missing secret, the entire TLSStore is rejected by Traefik — every cert in the `certificates` list is also unloaded. Traefik falls back to its built-in self-signed cert for ALL https requests.

Impact: prevents the newly issued *.kelsboi.dedyn.io wildcard (kelsboi-wildcard-tls) — and presumably the original *.knowledgedump.space serving — from working via SNI.

Options:
1. Fix Cloudflare API token / zone ID resolution so cert-manager can finish the knowledgedump-wildcard issuance (Probably the right fix; check ExternalSecret cloudflare-api-token in cert-manager ns and the ClusterIssuer config).
2. Temporarily flip TLSStore.spec.defaultCertificate to kelsboi-wildcard-tls so the store loads; existing knowledgedump.space hosts would lose their wildcard until #1 is fixed.

Detected during CILIUM/cert-manager work setting up DNS-01 for kelsboi.dedyn.io (commit 933036b). The deSEC webhook + Certificate are confirmed working — TLSStore distribution is the only blocker.
close_reason:
Fixed. Root cause: cert-manager's Cloudflare DNS-01 provider got stuck in cleanup with an empty zone ID path (/zones//dns_records/...) because the Cloudflare zone resolution failed transiently and the controller cached an empty zoneID, then looped forever trying to DELETE the TXT record without zone context. There were also 3 orphan _acme-challenge.knowledgedump.space TXT records in the Cloudflare zone (from this attempt + 2 from April) that confused the lego SOA/zone lookup. 

Cloudflare API token (1Password item 'cloudflare-dns', property 'password') verified valid + active via /user/tokens/verify, and has correct permissions: #zone:read, #dns_records:read, #dns_records:edit on zone knowledgedump.space (id 960eeb4fbbc31b09daac45333e1113e9). ESO + ClusterIssuer config is correct — no manifest changes needed.

Fix applied (no code changes):
1. Manually deleted 3 stale _acme-challenge.knowledgedump.space TXT records via CF API (the live one cert-manager was looping on, plus 2 orphans from April).
2. Deleted stuck Challenge + Order resources in traefik ns to force cert-manager to restart issuance cleanly.

Result:
- knowledgedump-wildcard cert: Ready=True (secret knowledgedump-wildcard-tls created)
- Traefik TLSStore 'default' now loads cleanly
- SNI test via port-forward confirms LE-issued certs served:
  * whoami.kelsboi.dedyn.io  -> CN=*.kelsboi.dedyn.io (LE R13)
  * whoami.knowledgedump.space -> CN=*.knowledgedump.space (LE R13)
  * unknown SNI -> defaultCertificate *.knowledgedump.space (no longer TRAEFIK DEFAULT CERT)

If this recurs (cert-manager getting stuck on Cloudflare cleanup), the workaround is: kubectl delete challenge -n <ns> <stuck-challenge> + kubectl delete order -n <ns> <stuck-order>, optionally cleaning orphan TXT records in the Cloudflare zone first. No user-side Cloudflare token changes required.

title: Incident retro: UPS fault → cluster-wide outage + XFS corruption (2026-05-09)
description:
On 2026-05-09 a UPS fault caused all 5 Talos nodes to power off uncleanly. The control plane (talos00) booted back into a stuck "Booting" state because EPHEMERAL XFS (/dev/sda4) corrupted during the unclean shutdown — kernel reported "Metadata has LSN (7413:30756) ahead of current LSN (7413:30281)", "log mount/recovery failed: error -117", and Talos's auto xfs_repair refused with "valuable metadata changes in a log which needs to be replayed". Talos has no auto `xfs_repair -L` and no in-cluster shell to run it manually.

No etcd snapshots existed (see TALOS-a8g), so recovery required a fresh bootstrap with full local-path PVC loss (Prometheus TSDB, Grafana, Graylog, OpenSearch, MongoDB, Nexus, etc.). GitOps (Flux + ArgoCD) reconciled application manifests but state-bearing PVCs were unrecoverable.

Known Talos issue: GH siderolabs/talos#9217, #8292 — XFS on bare metal Talos breaks on every power loss. Closed as "not planned".

This is a **post-incident analysis** task, not a fix task. Output is a recommendation memo + decision; implementation tickets get filed separately.
acceptance_criteria:
- Document timeline + root cause analysis
- Evaluate options and pick a path:
  1. Power resilience: redundant UPS (dual-feed, A/B power), UPS battery health check, NUT/apcupsd shutdown integration to gracefully `talosctl shutdown` before battery dies
  2. HA control plane: 3-master architecture (etcd quorum survives 1 node loss → no single-point XFS corruption disaster)
  3. Filesystem: switch EPHEMERAL from XFS to ext4 (Talos config supports this in newer versions; ext4 handles unclean shutdowns better)
  4. Combination: all of the above
- Cost/complexity tradeoff documented (extra UPS $, +2 control plane nodes RAM/CPU/electricity, filesystem migration risk)
- Decision recorded as ADR in docs/02-architecture/
- Implementation tickets filed for chosen path (one per change)</acceptance>
<parameter name="design">Key questions to answer:

**1. UPS strategy**
- What UPS do we have now? Single point of failure?
- NUT integration: Talos doesn't natively run NUT clients, but a sidecar / DaemonSet could call `talosctl shutdown` on low-battery signal
- Alternative: power monitor on a Pi that triggers shutdown via Talos API
- Cost: 2nd UPS ~$200-500

**2. 3-master architecture**
- Currently: 1 control plane (talos00) + 4 workers (talos01, talos02, talos03, talos06)
- Promoting 2 workers to control plane: lose ~2 nodes worth of workload capacity but gain etcd quorum (can lose 1 of 3 CPs without downtime)
- talos03 (Ryzen 5800U, idle) is a strong candidate per docs/05-projects/cluster-optimization/
- talos02 (Intel Ultra 5, 64GB) too capable to "waste" on CP role
- Best mix: talos00 + talos01 + talos03 as CPs

**3. Filesystem swap (XFS → ext4)**
- Talos machine config: `machine.disks` or `machine.systemDiskEncryption` doesn't directly cover EPHEMERAL FS choice
- Newer Talos may expose EPHEMERAL filesystem type. Need to verify current support
- Migration path: each node needs reset --system-labels-to-wipe=EPHEMERAL after config update — sequential, 1 at a time

**4. Combination**
The UPS issue and the etcd quorum issue are independent. Power problem → all 5 still drop. So even with 3 CPs, if ALL get power-killed, etcd corrupts on whichever one had ongoing writes.
Therefore: UPS+graceful-shutdown is the actual defense. HA CP is defense-in-depth for non-power failures (single disk failure, etc.).

**Recommendation (preliminary, validate during ticket work)**: All three. UPS + graceful-shutdown integration is highest leverage. 3-CP is defense in depth. Ext4 reduces blast radius if power-graceful fails.
notes: ADR-001 written: docs/02-architecture/ADR-001-power-resilience.md (commit 2355be7). Recommends A+B (UPS+NUT graceful-shutdown + 3-master HA); defers C (ext4 ephemeral). Awaits operator approval to file implementation tickets.
close_reason: Analysis complete: ADR-001 written (docs/02-architecture/ADR-001-power-resilience.md, commit 2355be7). Hardware UPS swap done. Implementation split into two children: TALOS-uu9 (UPS graceful-shutdown automation) and TALOS-awp (3-master HA control plane). ext4 ephemeral migration deferred per ADR.

title: Daily etcd snapshot CronJob with 10-snapshot retention
description:
Automate daily etcd snapshots so future control plane disasters (e.g., XFS EPHEMERAL corruption from power loss like the 2026-05-09 UPS fault) are recoverable without total cluster state loss.

Currently no etcd snapshots exist. After the UPS fault on 2026-05-09 corrupted the EPHEMERAL XFS partition on talos00, the only recovery path was a fresh bootstrap with full local-path PVC loss (Prometheus TSDB, Grafana, Graylog, OpenSearch, MongoDB, Nexus). Daily snapshots offloaded to durable storage would have allowed `talosctl bootstrap --recover-from=./db.snapshot` instead.

Snapshot creation: `talosctl -n <cp-ip> etcd snapshot <path>` (Talos's preferred consistent snapshot method, vs raw copy from /var/lib/etcd which lives on EPHEMERAL).

Reference: docs/02-architecture/dual-gitops.md, Sidero disaster recovery docs.
design:
Approach options to evaluate:
1. Kubernetes CronJob in cluster running `talosctl etcd snapshot` against the CP node — needs talosconfig secret, kubectl/talosctl image
2. Host-side cron on a separate machine with talosctl access — survives full cluster loss
3. Talos built-in scheduled snapshots if available in current version (v1.11.1)

Storage: NFS PVC (media or dedicated backup share). Local-path is unacceptable — defeats the purpose since it dies with EPHEMERAL.

Retention: simple `find -mtime +N -delete` or rclone/restic for offsite copy.

Bonus: also snapshot before any planned `talosctl upgrade` or config apply.
acceptance_criteria:
- CronJob runs daily, creates `talosctl etcd snapshot`
- Snapshots stored on NFS (NOT local-path, which dies with EPHEMERAL)
- Retention: keep last 10, prune older
- Alert on snapshot failure (Prometheus/Alertmanager)
- Documented restore procedure in docs/06-operations/ or similar
- Verified by manual test restore in non-prod or cluster rebuild
close_reason: Hourly etcd snapshot CronJob deployed (ConfigMap-tunable, distroless talosctl + mc upload, count-based retention, default 168). Test snapshot uploaded successfully (60MB, 25s wall time). PrometheusRule loaded into Mimir ruler with EtcdBackupJobFailed/NotRunning/Missing alerts. Manifests committed to talos-homelab main.

title: nebula-sync holds 6 of 16 pihole API seats on every replica
description:
Session census on all 5 pihole replicas (2026-09-11) shows remote_addr 10.244.3.163 (nebula-sync, user_agent curl/8.14.1) holding 6 valid API sessions on EVERY pod, out of a max_sessions of 16. That is ~38% of the seat pool per replica consumed by one client, leaving little headroom for the exporter, the Pi-hole CLI, and any human admin login.

nebula-sync runs every 300s (SYNC_INTERVAL=300) and appears to authenticate without reusing or releasing sessions. Sessions expire on the 1800s timeout (webserver.session.timeout), so 6 outstanding is the steady-state of ~1 new session per sync cycle x 6 cycles per timeout window — consistent with login-per-run and no logout.
notes:
FIX COMMITTED 4247b999 (pending deploy): sync.sh now releases every API seat after each cycle via remember_sid/release_sids, called from the main loop AFTER sync_once returns so it covers all five of sync_once's early-return paths.

VERIFY AFTER DEPLOY — this is the whole test:
  kubectl -n pihole exec pihole-1 -c pihole -- pihole api auth/sessions
then count valid sessions by remote_addr. nebula-sync (10.244.3.163, curl/8.14.1) should hold 0-1 seats, not 6. Expect total valid sessions per pod to drop from ~9-10 to ~3-4 of 16.
close_reason: Verified in prod 2026-09-11 22:36Z, 30min after deploy of 4247b999. nebula-sync now holds ZERO API seats on all five replicas (was 6 on every pod). Total valid sessions per pod dropped 9-10 -> 3 of 16; what remains is the exporter (2x Go-http-client on 127.0.0.1) and the Pi-hole CLI. title: Replace ekofr/pihole-exporter v1.2.0 — degrades with process uptime (TALOS-5292 root cause)
description:
WHY, stated honestly: this is justified by SESSION HYGIENE, not by the 10s latency bug. Do not close TALOS-5292 when this ships unless the latency is measured as fixed.

THE REAL, MEASURED PROBLEM THIS SOLVES:
webserver.session.timeout = 1800s and webserver.api.max_sessions = 16 (both confirmed via pihole-FTL --config). Per instance, inside one TTL window:
  exporter  @ 30s PodMonitor interval  = 60 logins
  nebula-sync @ SYNC_INTERVAL=300      =  6 logins
  -> ~66 sessions competing for 16 seats, roughly 4x oversubscribed.
Every pihole pod boots logging "Restored 9/10/11 API sessions" — leaked seats surviving restarts. ekofr/pihole-exporter is a v5-era exporter with a v6 shim: it logs in per scrape and never logs out. Upstream pi-hole/pi-hole#6102 ("API requests exhaust max_sessions") is this exact complaint; the visible symptoms are "API seats exceeded" on human web logins and 429s for scripted clients.

WHAT TO SWITCH TO — purpose-built v6 exporters, at least one of which reuses a single session across scrapes and caches responses, and one of which deletes its session on graceful shutdown (which is what stops seats leaking across pod restarts):
  https://github.com/Mosher-Labs/pihole6-exporter
  https://github.com/bazmonk/pihole6_exporter
  https://github.com/nbx3/pihole-exporter
Evaluate metric-name compatibility first: the pihole Grafana dashboard (infrastructure/base/monitoring/grafana-dashboards/resources/pihole.yaml) and any alerts are written against ekofr metric names (pihole_dns_queries_today, pihole_domains_being_blocked, pihole_status, ...). A swap that renames metrics silently blanks the dashboard.

WHAT THIS IS NOT:
Seat exhaustion is NOT the cause of the 10s scrape latency in TALOS-5292 — falsified 2026-09-11 by measurement: 101 minutes after a fresh roll (~200 exporter logins against 16 seats, 3+ TTL windows) latency was still 0.281s. Five theories are now dead there (wedge, inherently-slow, cross-node network, memory leak, seat exhaustion). Slow-onset over ~2.5 days remains unexplained and is being measured by an ad-hoc tracker pod.

ALSO CONSIDER, cheap and independent: raise webserver.api.max_sessions well above 16. It does not stop the churn but removes the oversubscription while the exporter swap is evaluated.

FILES: infrastructure/base/pihole/statefulset.yaml (exporter container), infrastructure/base/pihole/podmonitor.yaml (interval 30s + scrapeTimeout 25s), infrastructure/base/monitoring/grafana-dashboards/resources/pihole.yaml (metric names).
notes:
DONE in 94edb090 (pending deploy): sidecar swapped to ghcr.io/tomoconnor/pihole-exporter:1.3.1 pinned by digest sha256:32212fd2. Verified before adoption — identical 59-metric surface (zero dashboard/alert changes needed) and survives the wedge test that kills ekofr v1.2.0.

The original seat-leak premise of this bead turned out to be minor and is NOT what was fixed; the real defect was the wedge (see TALOS-5292). The dominant seat holder was nebula-sync, fixed separately in 4247b999 (TALOS-kl2c).

Close once deployed and verified in prod. Exit path from the fork is TALOS-3ccs.
close_reason: Done and verified. Sidecar swapped to ghcr.io/tomoconnor/pihole-exporter:1.3.1 pinned by digest (94edb090), deployed 2026-09-11. All five replicas answer /metrics in 0.27-0.35s; 574 tracker samples over 30min show zero stalls. Metric surface identical (59/59) so no dashboard or alert changes were needed. Exit from the fork is tracked in TALOS-3ccs.

title: pihole-exporter v1.2.0 degrades with process uptime (confirmed: fresh 0.14s vs sidecar 30s, same pihole)
description:
ROOT CAUSE UNKNOWN — this bead exists because the shipped fix is containment, not a cure.

On 2026-09-09 three of five pihole replicas (pihole-1/3/4, nodes talos01/talos00/talos03) had a dead exporter for >2 days. The container logged `starting pihole-exporter` and then nothing: port 9617 refused connections, the process never exited, restartCount stayed 0. Because the container had NO liveness or readiness probe, kubelet reported 2/2 Ready throughout and ServiceDown fired continuously. DNS was never affected.

ELIMINATED during diagnosis (do not re-investigate these):
 - Pi-hole v6 API/auth break: the two HEALTHY exporters return real data against pihole 2026.07.2 (dns_queries_today 434, domains_being_blocked 79995, status 1). v1.2.0 can talk to this version fine.
 - Startup race against the local pihole API: exporter start times do not correlate with outcome. Ordered 02:21:14 FAIL, 02:21:40 FAIL, 02:22:15 OK, 02:22:39 FAIL, 02:23:03 OK — pihole-2 started BEFORE pihole-1 and survived.
 - Local dependency down: all replicas, failing and healthy, answer HTTP 302 on 127.0.0.1:80/admin/.

REMAINING LEAD: the split is node-correlated (fail talos00/talos01/talos03, ok talos02-gpu/talos06) but n=5 is too small to conclude anything.

SHIPPED (containment): liveness + readiness probes on the exporter container, so a wedge self-heals in ~90s instead of persisting silently, and the Ready count stops lying.

TO DO: evaluate bumping ekofr/pihole-exporter off v1.2.0 — a process that hangs without exiting or serving is an upstream defect. Check the changelog for a fixed hang, or replace the exporter. If it recurs WITH probes in place, capture a goroutine dump / strace before the restart, since that is the evidence this investigation lacked.
notes:
DEPLOYED + VERIFIED SHORT-TERM 2026-09-11 22:36Z. 574 samples across 5 replicas over 30min: ZERO stalls (the one flagged row is http=000/ERR during the rollout restart, not a stall). Slowest genuine sample 0.839s. Before the fix, 2 of 5 replicas stalled 12-30s on EVERY sample.

DELIBERATELY LEFT OPEN. 30 minutes of green does not fully prove this in prod, and the reason is worth stating: the wedge only triggers when a scrape TIMES OUT. Responses have been healthy (0.27s) so no timeout has occurred, meaning the failure mode has not actually been exercised in production yet. What we do have is stronger than uptime: a controlled reproduction (3x curl -m 0.05 kills ekofr v1.2.0 permanently, leaves the fork at 0.144s) plus the upstream root cause in eko/pihole-exporter#332.

CLOSE WHEN: exporter-latency-tracker-hires shows zero stalls across several days AND at least one scrape timeout has occurred without wedging. Then delete the tracker (ad-hoc, NOT in GitOps):
  kubectl -n pihole logs exporter-latency-tracker-hires | awk -F, '$3>1'
  kubectl -n pihole delete pod exporter-latency-tracker-hires

ALSO FIX (latent bug found while investigating): native_sso reads authentik-immich-oidc but the authentik-ns Role get/patch resourceNames omits it ([authentik-zipline-oidc, private-app-sso-credentials, amberdark-outpost-token]) — immich-oidc get likely 403s. Add authentik-immich-oidc to resourceNames (and temporary-oidc if it's created in authentik ns).

title: Automate Authentik SSO app registration — feasibility (Kyverno/reflector/Terraform)
description:
INVESTIGATION (2026-09-09): can we stop hand-adding each SSO app in multiple places? Today adding a forward_single app touches: (1) a per-app blueprint block (provider+application+2 PolicyBindings), (2) the embedded-outpost provider UNION (!Find list in talos-private-blueprint.yaml), and (3) for a NEW blueprint file, the chart's fixed blueprints.configMaps mount list (helmrelease.yaml).

FINDINGS (authentik source/docs):
- Blueprints are DIRECTORY-DISCOVERED: authentik recursively walks blueprints_dir for *.yaml, monitors for new/changed files, applies every ~60min or on change. So any CM MOUNTED into that dir is auto-picked-up. The fixed list is a HELM-CHART mount limitation, not an authentik one.
- The embedded outpost's providers is an EXPLICIT list (OutpostSerializer providers=PrimaryKeyRelatedField many=True). No 'include all providers' toggle. Each proxy provider MUST be explicitly assigned. This is the real blocker.

VERDICT per touchpoint:
1. Per-app blueprint block: AUTOMATABLE via Kyverno generate (trigger on a label e.g. catalyst.io/sso on an IngressRoute or a small SSOApp CR; generate a ConfigMap with a data template parameterized by host+group).
2. Mounting the generated CM: PARTIAL — chart's fixed configMaps list won't mount it. Options: mount an emptyDir blueprints dir + a small sync sidecar that copies label-selected CMs in; or one pre-mounted aggregate CM Kyverno populates (1MB limit, awkward); or edit the list only when adding a new app-CLASS.
3. Outpost union: NOT cleanly Kyverno-able — appending to a list inside another CM's embedded YAML isn't a mutate/generate primitive. Needs either a tiny reconciler that lists proxy providers via the authentik API and PATCHes the embedded outpost (the 'custom API-Job' this repo deliberately avoided), or stays manual.

Reflector is the WRONG tool (mirrors secrets/CMs across namespaces; doesn't generate content or manage lists).

RECOMMENDATION / DECISION NEEDED:
- Idiomatic full-IaC answer is the authentik Terraform provider (authentik_provider_proxy + authentik_application + authentik_outpost with providers computed from a data source) — but that's a different toolchain than the GitOps blueprints.
- Within blueprints: highest-leverage low-toil step = a generator/template (or Kyverno generate) for the per-app block + switch the chart to a discovered blueprints dir so adding an app = drop one file; keep the outpost union as the single manual step OR a small reconciler.
- Kyverno mutating policy ALONE cannot fully automate it (outpost-union list-append + CM-mount limits). Pick: (A) Kyverno-partial + manual outpost union, (B) small authentik-API reconciler for the union, or (C) migrate SSO objects to the authentik Terraform provider.

title: yamllint has no .claude/ exclusion — every commit lints 20+ nested worktree copies
description:
'yamllint .' runs on every commit via lefthook pre-commit and takes ~151s, because .yamllint.yaml has no ignore entry for .claude/. Agent/workflow worktrees there are full repo checkouts, so every YAML in the repo gets linted once per worktree.

.markdownlint-cli2.yaml already excludes .claude and **/.claude; .prettierignore gained the same on 2026-09-06 (commit 0a9d095d). .yamllint.yaml is the remaining gap.

Fix: add .claude/ and **/.claude/ to the ignore block in .yamllint.yaml, and add .yamllint.yaml to the config list checked by 'task worktree:guard' in Taskfile.dev.yaml — that task currently checks only .prettierignore, .markdownlint-cli2.yaml and .gitignore, so it reports clean while this gap is open.

Secondary: yamllint reports pre-existing errors on committed files (e.g. infrastructure/base/cilium/lb-ipam.yaml 'too many blank lines'), and commits land regardless — worth deciding whether that gate should actually block.

title: Cowrie first-contact alerting: derive a metric from the log stream, do NOT add a Loki ruler blindly
description:
When the honeypot goes public (TALOS-ezcu) it will be scanned within minutes. An
alert confirming FIRST EXTERNAL CONTACT matters because the failure mode of this
system is silence, and silence is exactly what a broken port-forward looks like.

## ⚠️ THE OBSTACLE — there is no path to alert on Cowrie data today

Alerts in this cluster are PrometheusRule CRDs, synced by Alloy's
`mimir.rules.kubernetes` component into the MIMIR ruler. Cowrie's data is LOG
data in Loki. There is no Loki ruler and no `loki.rules.kubernetes` component
anywhere in the repo (checked). So no LogQL alert can currently be evaluated.

⚠️ DO NOT "just enable the Loki ruler" as the quick fix. `mimir.rules.kubernetes`
watches PrometheusRule CRDs CLUSTER-WIDE WITH NO SELECTOR. Adding a Loki ruler
fed by the same CRD kind means Mimir also ingests the LogQL rules and fails on
them. Any Loki-ruler work must add label selectors to BOTH sync components in
the same change.

## RECOMMENDED APPROACH — derive a counter, alert in Mimir

Add a `stage.metrics` block to the Alloy pipeline that already processes the
honeypot stream, emitting a counter labelled by src_ip class, e.g.
cowrie_events_total{eventid=...}, incremented only for lines whose src_ip is
NOT in 10.244.0.0/16. Then a normal PrometheusRule in
infrastructure/base/monitoring/v2-otel/baseline-alerts/ alerts on it. This
reuses the whole existing path and adds no new ruler.

⚠️ This touches the shared Alloy HelmRelease, which other workstreams also edit.
Coordinate; do not land it blind.

## WHAT TO ALERT ON — signal, not volume

DO NOT alert per session. A public SSH honeypot sees thousands of sessions a day
and per-session paging is unusable within an hour. Proposed, in descending order
of long-term value:

  1. FIRST CONTACT (one-shot, high value, then retire or mute): any external
     src_ip observed at all. Confirms the forward works. Expect it to fire within
     minutes of go-live. Its ABSENCE after ~1h is the real signal — consider
     inverting it into "no external traffic 6h after exposure" once live.
  2. cowrie.command.input from an external IP — an attacker got past auth and
     actually typed something. This is the genuinely interesting event and stays
     valuable long-term; volume is far lower than session counts.
  3. cowrie.login.success from an external IP, aggregated (rate, not per-event).
  4. Sensor-liveness inverse: honeypot stream silent for N hours while the pod is
     Ready — catches a rescheduled pod stranding the port-forward on the wrong
     node IP, which is the silent-failure mode this whole effort exists to avoid.

ASN-based novelty ("new source ASN") was considered and is NOT recommended: it
needs a GeoIP/ASN enrichment step that does not exist in this pipeline, and on a
public honeypot new ASNs arrive continuously, so it degrades into noise.

Route severity=warning to the existing `discord-default` receiver — no new
Alertmanager plumbing. Blocked on nothing, but only useful once TALOS-ezcu is done.

title: Pentest: DNS-tunnelling exfil from the honeypot egress path
description:
Prove or disprove that the honeypot's one permitted egress channel — DNS — can be abused to exfiltrate data past the default-deny policy. USER WANTS AN ACTIVE PENTEST, not just documentation.

## WHY THIS EXISTS

The Cowrie honeypot (TALOS-hg7, going public via TALOS-ezcu) locks egress to default-deny with
kube-dns:53 as the ONLY exception. That is the correct posture — it stops lateral movement,
outbound scanning, C2 and bulk exfil from a machine we are deliberately inviting attackers into.

⚠️ BUT DNS IS AN EXFIL CHANNEL. DNS tunnelling (iodine, dnscat2, dns2tcp, or hand-rolled TXT/A
query encoding) turns permitted name resolution into a bidirectional data path. An attacker who
compromises the container can encode stolen bytes into subdomain labels of queries that our own
CoreDNS will happily forward upstream. The default-deny egress does NOT close this — it is the
one hole we left open on purpose, and its abuse is exactly the gap worth measuring.

## THE PENTEST

From INSIDE the honeypot's network context (the honeypot pod, or a pod under the same
CiliumNetworkPolicy so the test reflects the real egress rules):

1. Establish whether arbitrary upstream DNS resolution is reachable at all, or whether CoreDNS
   only answers for in-cluster zones. This is the pivotal question — if CoreDNS does NOT forward
   arbitrary external queries, the channel may already be far narrower than assumed. Check the
   Corefile / CoreDNS ConfigMap for a forward/proxy block before running any tooling.
2. If external resolution IS forwarded: attempt a real DNS-tunnel exfil of a canary payload to a
   controlled resolver. Measure achievable throughput and whether it is detectable in existing
   telemetry (does Alloy/Loki see the query pattern? does anything alert?).
3. Assess detection and mitigation options WITHOUT breaking legitimate resolution:
   - CoreDNS query-rate limiting / response-size limits
   - egress DNS only to CoreDNS (already the case) vs also restricting what CoreDNS forwards
   - a NetworkPolicy or CoreDNS policy plugin that blocks external forwarding from the honeypot
     namespace specifically — the honeypot likely needs only in-cluster + the fake-fs resolution
     Cowrie fakes internally, so external DNS may be closable entirely for THIS namespace
   - detection: query-name entropy / length / volume anomaly rules

## SCOPE AND SAFETY

  - This is an AUTHORISED pentest of our OWN infrastructure. Exfil only a CANARY payload to a
    resolver you control. No real data.
  - Read-only against everything except the throwaway test pod. Do not change CoreDNS or the
    egress policy as part of the test — propose changes, the user applies them.
  - There is an existing honeypot pentest harness at
    infrastructure/base/honeypot/tests/pentest-job.yaml (marked 'do NOT GitOps-apply'). Check
    whether it is the right vehicle to extend rather than building new.

## DELIVERABLE

A clear yes/no on whether DNS exfil is possible from the honeypot as configured, the measured
throughput if so, whether it is currently detectable, and a concrete recommendation — ideally
'close external DNS forwarding for the honeypot namespace' if Cowrie does not need it.

Depends on the honeypot being deployed and hardened first (TALOS-hg7 / TALOS-ezcu). Part of the
TALOS-hg7 Security Ops epic.

comments.author: DJ Daniels
comments.text:
PIVOTAL QUESTION ANSWERED — CoreDNS DOES forward arbitrary external queries.

This ticket asks first whether upstream resolution is reachable at all, noting
the channel "may already be far narrower than assumed" if not. It is not
narrower. Measured 2026-08-24 from inside the honeypot pod's network namespace
(the logship sidecar shares the netns and the same CiliumNetworkPolicy):

    nslookup github.com  ->  140.82.116.3   (non-authoritative)

So the DNS tunnelling premise holds and step 2 of the pentest is worth running.
Supporting measurements from the same session:

  * Everything else really is closed. Blocked: talos06's own apid:50000,
    kubelet:10250 and apiserver:6443; all other nodes; kubernetes.default
    10.96.0.1:443; LAN gateway 192.168.1.1:80/443; 1.1.1.1:443; 8.8.8.8:53.
    Cilium blocks pod->own-node egress despite enable-host-firewall=false.
    DNS is genuinely the ONLY hole.
  * Bulk enumeration is NOT available — `any.any.svc.cluster.local` wildcard
    SRV returns NXDOMAIN on this CoreDNS.
  * But targeted resolution is a guess-and-confirm topology oracle:
    argocd-server.argocd, nexus.registry and postgres.cnpg-system all resolve.
    The attacker cannot connect to any of them, but can confirm they exist.

SCOPE NOTE: the exfil bandwidth question (step 2) is untested — I measured that
the channel is OPEN, not how much fits through it.

Candidate mitigation, NOT implemented (it is an egress change and therefore the
operator's call): a Cilium L7 DNS rule on allow-dns-egress restricting
matchPattern to *.cluster.local. That closes both the exfil path and the
topology oracle, at the cost of cowrie being unable to resolve external names —
which it has no legitimate need to do, since it cannot reach the internet anyway.

title: Remove the stale kubernetes-service-endpoints KSM series, or confirm the scrape job is intentionally retired
description:
Found while building TALOS-l407's alert rules.

kube-state-metrics is currently scraped by exactly one job (job="kube-state-metrics"). But a SECOND job, job="kubernetes-service-endpoints", also collected KSM until roughly 2026-08-07 and its series are still inside Mimir's retention.

The two use DIFFERENT label schemas, and that is the dangerous part:
  job="kube-state-metrics"          -> namespace="media-private"
  job="kubernetes-service-endpoints" -> namespace="monitoring", exported_namespace="media-private"

The stale copy overwrites the real namespace with the SCRAPER's namespace. An instant query looks clean because those series are no longer ingested, so this is invisible in normal use. Any range or lookback query long enough to reach before ~2026-08-07 resurrects them.

MEASURED: an unpinned 30d duration query on whisparr returned BOTH 17.4 days (phantom) and its true 4 minutes.

Every rule in workload-readiness-alerts.yaml and every new panel in the workload-ops fleet-triage row now pins job="kube-state-metrics" for exactly this reason, and both files document it. But the trap remains for anyone writing a new dashboard panel or rule against kube_* metrics with a long lookback, and it will keep biting until the stale series age out of retention (Mimir compactor_blocks_retention_period is 8760h = 1 YEAR, so this does not self-heal any time soon).

WORK:
  1. Confirm the kubernetes-service-endpoints job no longer scrapes KSM (it appears already removed -- find where it was defined and confirm it was deliberate).
  2. Decide whether to delete the stale series from Mimir (ruler/compactor delete API) rather than carry the trap for a year.
  3. Audit existing dashboards/rules for unpinned kube_* selectors with long lookbacks.

Related: TALOS-l407.
notes:
Confirmed independently by the team lead: this is the trap that would have silently broken the new workload-readiness rules.

KSM was scraped by a SECOND job (kubernetes-service-endpoints) until ~2026-08-07. Those series
put the real namespace in 'exported_namespace' and overwrite 'namespace' with 'monitoring' (the
scraper's own ns). They are no longer ingested, so INSTANT queries look perfectly clean — only a
lookback resurrects them.

Measured: an unpinned 30d duration query on whisparr returned 17.4 DAYS of phantom downtime
alongside its true 4 minutes. Unpinned, alert rules would report real outages against the WRONG
NAMESPACE.

⚠️ Mimir retention is 8760h, so this does NOT age out for a year. Every kube_* selector needs
job="kube-state-metrics" pinned. The new rules and dashboard panels all do.

title: immich-video-faces: adapt to VectorChord after the immich vector migration
description:
Companion to TALOS-cibi / talos-private TALOS-0lf (immich pgvecto.rs -> VectorChord).
Researched read-only 2026-08-24. Repo: /Users/panda/catalyst-devspace/workspace/immich-video-faces

## HEADLINE: this is NOT the breaking change it looked like

IVF talks to immich's postgres DIRECTLY (k8s/service-postgres.yaml -> Service immich-postgres,
selector app: immich, port 5432 = the postgres sidecar inside the immich pod). It reads and
WRITES vector data. So the concern was right to raise. But its SQL is portable:

  - VectorChord is built ON pgvector and reuses pgvector's types. Both pgvecto.rs and pgvector
    name the type 'vector' and define the '<=>' cosine-distance operator with the same 0..2
    semantics.
  - db.py INSERT_EMBEDDING uses %s::vector(512) and SEARCH_FACES uses fs.embedding <=> %s::vector(512).
    web/queries.py:256,318,323 use fs1.embedding <=> fs2.embedding. All valid unchanged.
  - The unqualified name resolves correctly: search_path is set at DATABASE level to
    '"$user", public, vectors', and public precedes vectors, so post-migration 'vector' binds to
    public.vector (pgvector) and not vectors.vector. No ambiguity error.
  - db.py:160 get_connection -> pgvector.psycopg register_vector does TypeInfo.fetch(conn,'vector'),
    which is to_regtype() and therefore resolves by search_path precedence, not ambiguously.
    It is also effectively decorative here: IVF string-builds "[a,b,c]" and casts explicitly
    (db.py:207, db.py:218) and never SELECTs an embedding column back, so the binary adapter is
    never on the path.
  - schema.py EXPECTED_SCHEMA face_search.embedding = "USER-DEFINED" stays correct;
    information_schema reports USER-DEFINED for both extensions.
  - IVF's extra table video_face_scan_log survives: immich getSchemaDrift() uses
    tables:{ignoreExtra:true}, and drift is a WARN not a boot failure.

Also verified live that immich migration 1780435471692-DeleteMismatchedAssetFaces (deletes
asset_face rows where person.ownerId != asset.ownerId) matches 0 rows here, so it will not
touch IVF's injected faces. IVF's assign_person already scopes its search by the asset's ownerId.

IVF HAS ALREADY RUN IN PROD: video_face_scan_log has 172 rows and 23134 of the 23146 asset_face
rows sit on IVF-scanned assets. Essentially the entire face corpus is IVF-produced. It is
preserved by the migration (values are cast through real[], not regenerated).

## WHAT ACTUALLY NEEDS CHANGING

1. web/queries.py:356 get_immich_safety_report()
   SELECT extversion FROM pg_extension WHERE extname IN ('vector','vectors')
   -> add 'vchord'. Post-migration BOTH vchord and vector are installed, and fetchone() picks
   one arbitrarily, so return all rows and report them. Rename the report key off "pgvector"
   or keep it and add the extension name. Verdict logic at queries.py:424 keys off
   report["pgvector"]["installed"] and would currently go "danger" if it ever missed.
   Frontend follows: frontend/src/components/DiagnosticsPanel.tsx:87-92 and
   frontend/src/stores/types.ts:73.

2. NEW: vchordrq probe handling in db.py SEARCH_FACES.
   immich creates the index as USING vchordrq (embedding vector_cosine_ops) with lists sized by
   targetListCount(): lists = 1 for any table under 128,000 rows, and it sets
   ALTER DATABASE immich SET vchordrq.probes = 1, then overrides per query with
   `set local vchordrq.probes = ceil(lists/8)` inside a transaction
   (search.repository.ts:314,350).
   At today's 23,145 face rows lists=1, so probes=1 already scans the whole single list and
   recall is fine — no action needed to ship.
   BUT once face_search crosses 128,000 rows immich reindexes with more lists, and IVF's
   connections will silently fall back to the database default probes=1 and lose recall on
   face matching, with no error. Mirror immich: wrap SEARCH_FACES in a transaction with
   `SET LOCAL vchordrq.probes = <n>`, or given IVF's tiny result set just force exact search
   with `SET LOCAL enable_indexscan = off`. Cheap now, invisible bug later.

3. Dev/test envs still pin the dead combination and are broken the same way prod was:
   docker-compose.dev.yml:6      tensorchord/pgvecto-rs:pg16-v0.2.0
   tilt/dev-immich-stack.yaml:28 tensorchord/pgvecto-rs:pg16-v0.2.0
   Both also run immich-server:release FLOATING, which now resolves to v3.1.0 -> instant
   "No vector extension found". Swap both to
   ghcr.io/immich-app/postgres:16-vectorchord0.4.3-pgvector0.8.1-pgvectors0.2.1
   to match what prod will become.

4. Forward coupling for TALOS-hx77.10 (CNPG): k8s/service-postgres.yaml selects app: immich.
   When immich's postgres is extracted to a CNPG Cluster that selector breaks and the Service
   must be repointed at the CNPG -rw service. Cross-repo, note it there too.

## SHIP ORDER: TALOS-b9i BEFORE the migration

Ship it first. Nothing in b9i is invalidated by the migration — IVF's SQL is unchanged by it,
and b9i is purely the "create the GH repo, push 3 repos in order, verify ArgoCD sync" runbook
with all files already staged and kustomize building clean. Holding a P0 behind a DB migration
buys nothing. It also gives a deployed baseline plus IVF's own /diagnostics safety report to
verify the migration against.

One operational caveat: k8s/cronjob.yaml runs `run --batch-size 10` daily at 03:00 and will
open write connections. Suspend that CronJob for the migration window so nothing inserts into
face_search while immich is doing the ALTER COLUMN / reindex, then unsuspend and confirm the
safety report reads vchord.

Items 1 and 2 are follow-ups AFTER the migration lands, not blockers for b9i.
notes:
Vector migration is COMPLETE as of 2026-08-24 — immich now runs vchord 0.4.3 + vector 0.8.1, embedding columns are public.vector, face_index and clip_index are both vchordrq. So this ticket's changes are no longer anticipatory; they apply to the CURRENT state.

⚠️ Item 1 (web/queries.py:356) is now ACTIVELY WRONG rather than merely future-facing: the check
lists ('vector','vectors') and BOTH vchord and vector are installed, so fetchone() picks one
arbitrarily and 'vectors' no longer exists at all.

Item 2 (vchordrq probes) remains latent — face_search is 23,145 rows and lists=1, so probes=1
already scans the whole single list and recall is fine. It breaks silently past 128,000 rows.

⚠️ BLOCKING CONTEXT: immich-video-faces has ZERO COMMITS and NO REMOTE (see TALOS-b9i). Any
change made to it right now exists only as an uncommitted file on one Mac.

title: [bug] whisparr CrashLoops on liveness probe — app healthy, likely CPU-throttled
description:
media-private/whisparr has been 0/1 for 136m with 3 restarts, exit code 137 (SIGKILL).

NOT the floating-tag bug, despite the tag. Its image is
ghcr.io/hotio/whisparr:latest@sha256:c97884f746e7209c42412fb1cdcc232c9711d273675e1ebb96df9da2225aadd5
— :latest but DIGEST-PINNED, so imagePullPolicy IfNotPresent is safe there. Digest pinning
makes the tag irrelevant. Worth noting because it looks like a TALOS-6gnx casualty and is not.

NOT OOM either: lastState reason is Error, not OOMKilled, and it is using 70Mi against a 512Mi
limit.

THE APP ITSELF IS FINE. Logs show a clean start:
  Microsoft.Hosting.Lifetime: Now listening on: http://[::]:6969
  Microsoft.Hosting.Lifetime: Application started.
  GithubUpdatePackageProvider: Current version '2.2.0.108' is up-to-date
Migrations complete, no errors. It then gets SIGKILLed.

So the liveness probe is failing and kubelet is killing a healthy process:
  Liveness:  http-get http://:http/ping delay=60s timeout=20s period=30s failure=6
  Readiness: http-get http://:http/ping delay=30s timeout=5s period=10s failure=3
  containerPort 6969, name=http   <- the port DOES resolve, so it is not a misnamed port

LIKELY CAUSE — CPU throttling: requests cpu 10m, limits cpu 300m, and it is currently using
183m. A .NET app under a tight CPU limit can miss a 5s readiness timeout while still serving.
The 10m request is also far below actual usage, so the scheduler is placing it as if it were
idle.

FIRST THINGS TO CHECK:
  1. Whether /ping is even a valid endpoint on Whisparr v2 — the *arr apps vary here, and some
     need /ping while others expose only /api/v3/system/status with an API key.
  2. Raise the cpu request toward observed usage (~200m) and the limit above it, then see if
     the probe stops failing.

⚠️ OWNED BY A SISTER REPO, NOT THIS ONE: annotation
argocd.argoproj.io/tracking-id = arr-stack-private:apps/Deployment:media-private/whisparr,
sourced from git@github.com:TheBranchDriftCatalyst/talos-private.git. The fix belongs there.
Do not patch it live — ArgoCD will revert it.
